title: Rhapsody in Blue
hook: A clarinet slides up into the Jazz Age, and a Broadway songwriter becomes a concert composer in one afternoon.

painting.title: Nocturne in Black and Gold: The Falling Rocket
painting.pairingNote: Ira Gershwin named the Rhapsody after seeing an exhibition of Whistler’s paintings, which carry musical titles like this one; a night of scattered fireworks that critics called formless, as some later called the Rhapsody.

facts: In January 1924 George Gershwin, a 25-year-old Broadway songwriter, read in a newspaper that he was writing a “jazz concerto” for the bandleader Paul Whiteman. He had turned the idea down; Whiteman talked him round, and the concert was five weeks away.

Gershwin said the shape of the piece came to him on a train to Boston, in its rattle and rhythm: “a sort of musical kaleidoscope of America”. He wrote it for two pianos; Whiteman’s arranger Ferde Grofé scored it for the band, finishing eight days before the concert. His brother Ira suggested the title after visiting an exhibition of paintings by Whistler.

It was first played on 12 February 1924 at Aeolian Hall in New York, at a long concert called “An Experiment in Modern Music”, with Gershwin at the piano. He improvised part of his solo and wrote it down only later. The audience cheered; the critics were divided.

It is a [[rhapsody|rhapsody]]: one movement, free in form, made of contrasting episodes rather than a plan. It mixes the concerto with jazz, ragtime and Broadway song, and its melodies are coloured by bent [[blue-note|blue note]]s.
bigPicture.inOneLine: a clarinet’s wail, a city’s bustle, one big slow tune, and a blazing return to the start.

movements.heading: Rhapsody in Blue
movements.tempo: Molto moderato, with many changes of tempo
movements.summary: One movement of about a quarter of an hour, played without a break. Piano and orchestra take turns: the orchestra announces a tune, the piano takes it apart in long solos, and the music keeps changing speed and mood. Halfway through, the bustle stops for one long, slow melody, which returns at full strength near the end.

mainIdeas.name: The opening theme
mainIdeas.description: the clarinet’s rising wail and the bluesy, jaunty tune that follows. It comes back throughout the piece.

mainIdeas.name: The “train” tune
mainIdeas.description: a quick, chugging, repeated idea, light and percussive.

mainIdeas.name: The slow tune
mainIdeas.description: a broad, warm melody for the strings, the most famous moment after the opening.

stops.hear: A low clarinet trill, then a long upward slide, ending in a cheeky, bluesy tune
stops.happening: The opening theme. The [[glissando|glissando]] began as a joke by Whiteman’s clarinettist in rehearsal, and Gershwin kept it

stops.hear: A [[muted|muted]] trumpet answers; then the full orchestra plays the tune, swaggering
stops.happening: The band takes over the theme

stops.hear: The piano alone: flourishes, stops and starts, the opening tune in pieces
stops.happening: The first long piano solo, written to sound improvised

stops.hear: A quick, chugging tune; the orchestra and the piano toss it between them
Short scenes one after another: brass outbursts, piano solos that hesitate and joke, sudden changes of speed
stops.happening: The middle of the rhapsody, a string of episodes

stops.hear: The orchestra builds to a loud climax, then calms and slows
stops.happening: The approach to the slow tune

stops.hear: The strings, warm and slow, play a long, singing melody
The piano takes the slow tune, softly and freely, then the orchestra again
stops.happening: The slow tune on the piano, with plenty of [[rubato|rubato]]

stops.hear: Fast and nervous: hammered piano chords and runs, the band pushing ahead
stops.happening: The quick section before the end; Gershwin’s piano at its most percussive

stops.hear: The whole orchestra plays the slow tune at full power, grand and broad
stops.happening: The slow tune as the climax, *Grandioso*

stops.label: Last 40 seconds
stops.hear: Brass and piano blare out the opening theme; a last loud B-flat chord

notice: Listen to the very first notes. Many clarinettists make the slide sound like a voice, a wail rather than a scale.
Count how often the opening tune comes back, in different speeds and colours. It holds the loose structure together.
Grofé’s scoring includes saxophones and a banjo, instruments from the dance band rather than the symphony orchestra. Listen for the saxophones in the band passages.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: Bernstein plays the piano and conducts at the same time. The Columbia Symphony Orchestra was a recording orchestra that Columbia Records assembled from New York players for sessions; it plays a version for full symphony orchestra, based on Grofé’s later scoring, not the 1924 jazz-band original.

threads.title: A concert for jazz
threads.body: Whiteman’s concert set out to show that jazz could stand in a concert hall. The Rhapsody was the second-to-last item on a long programme, and it was the one people remembered.

threads.title: Loose by design
threads.body: Critics then and later found the piece formless. Leonard Bernstein, who loved it, wrote in 1955 that you could cut out parts of it and it would still be the *Rhapsody in Blue*. Its unity comes from its themes, which return again and again, not from a classical plan.

threads.title: New York
threads.body: Gershwin heard the piece in a train’s rattle and called it a portrait of America’s “metropolitan madness”. It has been linked to New York ever since, from Woody Allen’s *Manhattan* to *Fantasia 2000*.
